poc_summary: A deterministic script (/poc/gen_and_run.sh) generates a wasm-GC module (via python, identical bytes every run) with 8 struct types of 10000 i64 fields each (640,000 bytes total, exceeding the default 512KiB GC heap), and 8 globals whose const-expr initializers are `struct.new_default $tN`. It then runs `wasmtime run -W gc=y -W function-references=y` on that module. The last global's allocation exceeds the fixed-capacity GC heap, so `StructRef::_new` returns `Err("GC heap out of memory")` during global initialization (`initialize_vmctx_globals` in instance.rs), exercising exactly the code path named in the root cause (newly-reachable fallible GC allocation inside const-expr evaluation, hit via the pre-existing unconditional `eval(...).expect(...)` in the global initializer).
explanation: Built pre_intro (bf06c66ddd3f), post_intro (128e6b8f57b6), and post_benign (bf06c66ddd3f + companion patch) with sanitizers in Docker. Inspected const_expr.rs and instance.rs: pre_intro's ConstOp enum has no StructNew/StructNewDefault variants at all (GC struct allocation is unreachable from const-expr); the intro commit adds these variants, routing them through the fallible StructRef::_new, while the existing global-initializer call site in instance.rs (`initialize_vmctx_globals`) still does `const_evaluator.eval(&mut context, init).expect("should be a valid const expr")` unconditionally — exactly the stated root cause. No PoC/run.sh existed, so I crafted a deterministic generator script producing a WasmGC module whose defined globals use `struct.new_default` on struct types large enough in aggregate to exceed the fixed 512KiB default GC heap capacity, guaranteeing the last global's `StructRef::_new` call returns `Err`. Running the identical script via run_poc against all three builds gives: pre_intro -> graceful module-parse rejection (opcode doesn't exist pre-intro, confirming the panic isn't a generic/unrelated input-parsing artifact); post_intro -> a genuine Rust panic at the exact `.expect()` site named in meta.json; post_benign -> the same underlying GC-OOM condition surfaces as a cleanly propagated `anyhow::Error` with no panic. This satisfies the LogicError oracle: a precise, self-checking, target-exercising reproduction with exact distinguishing output lines recorded identically (same command/content) for all three revisions.

oracle.benign_marker: Error: failed to run main module ... Caused by: 0: failed to instantiate ... 1: GC heap out of memory (exit=1, clean propagated error, no panic)
oracle.description: Same generated module + same `bash /poc/gen_and_run.sh` (-> `wasmtime run -W gc=y -W function-references=y`) run via run_poc against pre_intro, post_intro, and post_benign builds. Distinguishing signal: presence/absence of a Rust panic (`thread 'main' panicked ...`, process exit 101) vs. a clean propagated `anyhow::Error` (process exit 1) reporting the identical underlying "GC heap out of memory" condition.
oracle.target_evidence: Backtrace in post_intro: StructRef::_new -> ConstEvalContext::struct_new -> ConstExprEvaluator::eval -> Instance::new, with the panic resolving to instance.rs:1283:18, exactly the `.expect("should be a valid const expr")` call on `const_evaluator.eval(&mut context, init)` inside `initialize_vmctx_globals` named in meta.json's root_cause/findings. post_benign reaches the identical GC-heap-out-of-memory condition (same backtrace frames) but returns it as a normal `Result` error instead of panicking, matching fix_commit 7941919851b8 (removing unwrap/expect on const-expr eval results in favor of `?`).
